speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege.
During the meeting of the committee on agriculture in Winnipeg, held on April 18 in the Monarch Life Building, the chairman of the committee tried by devious means to stop the opposition from making itself heard.
As I wanted to ask, in the presence of the representatives of the Wheat Pool, the Saskatchewan Wheat Board and the Western Farmers, that the Winnipeg Grain Exchange which is exploiting Canadian farmers be abolished, the chairman of that committee denied me the right to speak.
So I submit that this committee should resume that sitting, in Ottawa, with all the representatives who were in Winnipeg attending, to prevent this time the use of such devious means.
I put forward this proposal in order to know the true exploiters in the grain trade.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: REPORT ON FIFTH CANADA-JAPAN MINISTERIAL MEETING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to table the joint communique of the fifth meeting of the Canada-Japan ministerial committee and to report very briefly to the
house on the very useful meetings which were held in Tokyo last week.
This ministerial committee is not a negotiating body but rather a means whereby ministers from the two countries can from time to time exchange views on the full range of bilateral relations between Canada and Japan, as well as on the international situation. The fact that Japan is Canada's third largest trading partner, now competing for second place, is in itself sufficient reason for periodic and high level discussions between Canadian ministers and their Japanese counterparts.
The need for and the utility of these meetings is enhanced by the increasingly close co-operation between Canada and Japan in political and other fields, both bilaterally and in all the major international organizations to which we both belong. Most of all however the meetings form an important part of Canada's role as a Pacific as well as an Atlantic country, and they also reflect the growing Canadian activities throughout the Pacific area.
I have taken part in three meetings of this committee in different capacities and, in my view, the one just completed is the most useful to date, in large part due to the increasing easiness of discussions over a broad range of subjects. This is not to suggest that we found a complete identity of views with the Japanese. We did not, and, where we differed, we both made clear where our differences lay. On bilateral matters, for example, as you will see from the communique, the Canadian ministers spoke with some vigour about certain Japanese trade restrictions which are causing difficulties for some Canadian exports. But one advantage of these meetings is to enable ministers to speak directly with their Japanese opposite numbers on matters which are of great concern to Canada.
[DOT] (2:10 p.m.)
In addition to expressing my satisfaction over the quality of the discussions, both formal and informal, which we held with our Japanese colleagues, I should like to express our thanks for the warm and generous hospitality offered by our hosts. We were able to visit certain areas outside the capital and to

get some impression of the cultural and industrial aspects of Japan. We visited the site of Expo '70 at Osaka and saw the Canadian pavilion, its outward structure now almost completed, and the pavilions of British. Columbia, Ontario and Quebec. The extent of Canadian participation in this world exhibition, and the fact that our visit coincided with a tour of Japan by the Toronto Symphony Orchestra are, I believe, further indications of the broadening and deepening of our relations.
It is of interest that a special newspaper supplement marking the visit was issued on the day our meetings began. The relationship between Canada and Japan is, I am convinced, a relationship which contains great mutual benefits and1 which in itself makes some contribution to stability and economic development in Asia and the Pacific region.

I also hope the minister will be able to tell us whether he had any success in reaching an agreement with Japan to allow Canadian rapeseed into Japan on the same basis that United States soyabeans are admitted, because we are operating at a great disadvantage in this market.

subsubtopic: REPORT ON FIFTH CANADA-JAPAN MINISTERIAL MEETING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are happy to hear from the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) that the Canadian mission to Japan has been fruitful.
Having visited Japan myself in January, I noticed that trade agreements1, co-operation and goodwill between Canada and Japan could be quite beneficial to our country.
During my trip, I noticed that the Japanese citizen was practising what President Kennedy said and repeated: Ask not what your country can do for you; ask what you can do for your country.
Japan has a population of 100 million inhabitants. It is a populous country but not that much compared with other great countries.
Despite that, it is developing at an incredible speed in every field of economic activity.
The Canadian ministers must have realized that the more relations we have with Japan, the more we will benefit from them. I sincerely believe that we have everything to gain by having more contacts with that country than we may have had with certain European countries in the past, because we have more to learn from Japan than from Europe, from every point of view. I suggest that our commercial and cultural relations with Japan must be improved.
I have also noticed that the ministers discussed just about everything with their Japanese counterparts during their stay in that country. They discussed the wheat trade, for example, and I felt at a certain point, while I was in western Canada, that the five, six or seven ministers sent to Japan could have liquidated the actual wheat surplus in the western provinces and shipped a good part of it to those who need it, particularly to Japan.
Mr. Speaker, we are happy to see that Canada is taking the necessary steps to initiate and maintain closer and more extensive relations with Japan, and I am convinced that our two countries will greatly benefit from it.

6.	Have complaints been received, by the department regarding excessive use of corporal punishment, from parents or teachers and, if so, what action was taken by the department to investigate or correct the situation?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: CORPORAL PUNISHMENT IN N.W.T. AND YUKON SCHOOLS
speechtext:
1. In
both the Yukon Territory and Northwest Territories, limited corporal punishment is permitted.
2.	This department does not formulate corporal punishment policy in the Yukon. Rather, the territorial government, in conjunction with the school administrators, set the policy. In the Northwest Territories policy is formulated in accordance with the N.W.T. School Ordinance and Regulations, in consultation with the school principals.
3.	A correction strap is permitted.
4.	In the Yukon, corporal punishment may be administered by either the principal or teacher, but only in the presence of the principal and with his permission. In the Northwest Territories, either the principal or the teacher may administer the punishment.
5.	There is a laid down policy for recording corporal punishment in the Mackenzie District. Although there is no over-all requirement for records to be kept in either the Arctic district or the Yukon, individual schools do maintain such records.
6.	No complaints have been received by the Department with regard to the Yukon. In the Mackenzie District two complaints have been received in the past seven years; both complaints were investigated, and in each case the teacher involved in the incident received a reprimand. In the Arctic District one complaint was received from a teacher regarding another teacher who allegedly struck children in the classroom. This complaint was investigated by the District Superintendent of Schools, the Regional Superintendent of Schools, and by a representative of the Northwest Territories Teachers' Association; however, the allegations were not adequately substantiated.

The house resumed, from Friday, April 18, consideration of Bill C-150, an act to amend the Criminal Code, the Parole Act, the Penitentiary Act, the Prisons and Reformatories Act and to make certain consequential amendments to the Combines Investigation Act, the Customs Tariff and the National Defence Act, as reported (with amendments) from the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs. And the motion of Mr. McQuaid (for Mr. Woolliams):
That Bill C-150, an act to amend the Criminal Code, the Parole Act, the Penitentiary Act, the Prisons and Reformatories Act and to make certain

consequential amendments to the Combines Investigation Act, the Customs Tariff and the National Defence Act, be amended by Inserting in clause 7, after the word "age" on line 9, page 24, the following words:
"except as to bestiality and carnal copulation with a beast".

Mr. Speaker, last Friday we were still dealing with the famous clause 7 of this bill, which we wanted deleted, in view of its ambiguity, and above all-these are the points that were debated at length last week-the fact that it fails to take into account the views from our ridings. In fact, its passing would be opposed to the dignity of the human beeing.
Mr. Speaker, that is the reason why we keep on insisting and we would like to hear others, particularly members of the government, express their views and those of their constituents on this clause now before us.
We spoke about everything and we finally find this section so stupid and ridiculous that we wonder how such views could possibly be submitted in a place as dignified as this house.
The hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Fortin), who spoke Friday on this amendment has just explained that because we did not get our way with the first amendments, we will at least make an attempt to improve somewhat this legislation. We want some points to be explained, and that is the purpose of this amendment.
These ridiculous and stupid things are leading the debate into dog houses, cow stables and pig pens, as we are now dealing with bestiality. It is imperative to respect human dignity, in such a way that the law will provide for the most freakish cases, too bestial for human beings. That is the purpose of this amendment.
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)
We want that problem to be examined seriously and hope that we have heard the last of the argument that the clause before us only serves to sanction something which is quite normal, undercover of the right to liberty. Mr. Speaker, we fail to see how individual freedom can be improved by saying that an act which is now considered criminal in itself will be accepted from now on because two persons committing it are 21 years of age. We believe that the passing of such a legislation is useless.
At least we would like the amendment to be made more specific by adding the words
April 21, 1969

"except as to bestiality and carnal copulation with a beast."
Mr. Speaker, we have now reached the point where we do not know whether we are protecting the animals rather than man through this amendment. Whatever it may be, the discussion requires that we point it out.
Mr. Speaker, it would be really important that the majority of the hon. members express their own opinion freely, because we believe that we should not rely on the vote. Recently, I happened to be explaining that, but my time elapsed before I could finish. I readily understood what was meant by "free vote". To speak of a free vote implies the existence of votes which are not. That struck me as rather odd. However, on seeing how the "voting machine" works, one finally understands what the expression "free vote" means.
If government members cannot have a free vote, they could at least rise and explain their reasons for voting in favour of the bill. If they do not want to do so, if they are not against homosexuality, they should at least have the courage to rise and tell us why they are for it. We have not heard from them yet.
We are aware of the opinions of our good neighbours of the New Democratic party who, under the guise of liberty, are generally in favour of such legislation. At least, they have clearly expressed their opinions. We respect them even though we do not agree with them.
However on the government side-we know it because we are told so behind the scenes and because we know their constituents who, incidentally are preparing to vote for the Ral-liement creditiste-they should express the opinion of the population on that matter.
That is what we would like to know. It is the role of this parliament to reflect public opinion through the people's representatives here, and I wonder if it makes sense that some hon. members should remain silent under the pretext that those are minor questions and that an actual and well-established situation must be clarified.
Even if 10, 15 or 20 per cent of the population were suffering of that so-called disease, homosexuality, it should in no way justify its legalization, and I wonder where one can find arguments to justify it? We should like to hear reasonable arguments.
When we are told that such a condition is due to an illness, we are quite in agreement; but if it is something that concerns mental or physical health, we should, I think, be logical

and admit the true significance of the figures supplied by the experts.
Less than 1 per cent of homosexuals are truly sick while the rest are nothing more nor less than vicious people.
The younger ones are corrupted and raped by older ones. It is merely the decline of morality that accounts for the higher percentage of cases. If this house intends to legalize such acts when they are committed by persons 21 years of age and over, one must admit that it is legalizing a vice.
Let us see things as they are. As a matter of fact, if we were dealing with a medical problem, we would organize psychiatric clinics in order to cure these sick people, as is being done for alcoholics, the mentally ill and the handicapped. Why not try to cure these people instead of legalizing a loathsome act?
The other day, I mentioned kleptomania, as an example, but I was not taken seriously, I think. So, I will give it another try.
Even though a number of kleptomaniacs are not responsible for their actions because they are prompted to commit them by a morbid impulse, is it a reason for us to legalize theft for persons aged 21 years or over under the pretext that they suffer from kleptomania?
That is exactly what we are doing with respect to homosexuality. We approve of indecent, even criminal acts. It is an indictable offence in that it leads youth astray, relaxes morals, brings about decadence, causes disorders and paves the way to anarchy.
Mr. Speaker, perhaps this is one of the causes of the type of anarchy now prevailing. When one sees young people with energy to spare looking at their elders with a critical eye, wrangling and protesting and even committing acts of vandalism as a manifestation of their anarchic minds, it is because they do not accept the society that we prepared for them.
Are such bills likely to help us check this anarchictic movement?
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
Is that the example we set for the young people of the country? Is that the way to encourage our young people to put forth their energy for the common good of all? It certainly is not.
Indeed, what will the public reaction be when this bill is passed? I hope it is not.

The distinctions that are made here, tor instance, are not always made elsewhere. The people, generally, do not take time to make the required distinctions and reservations. And so, what happens? In the eyes of the public, those of the young people of Canada, one thing will be legalized: homosexuality. There will always be professional go-betweens who will give 18-year olds cards proving that the bearer is 21. These things are being done.
As identification cards are still not compulsory, it will be difficult to tell who is 21 and who is 20, 11 months and 30 days. The latter will be sent to prison while the former will go free. To say that homosexuality is legal from 21 years of age on is erroneous.
The consequences of this bill must be analyzed. If, as I have said before, we are dealing here with a sickness, then let the Department of Health take care of it and not the Department of Justice.
As for the disastrous consequences of the passage of this clause for all our young people, they should be fully looked into. Indeed we must keep our youth wholesome and set them patterns to follow. We must be their models. Canadian Parliament must not set bad examples to all this youth which expects much more from us.
In fact, young people expect to be given the opportunity to develop their initiative. They wish to make full use of their energies. They are ready to work to attain their ideals, in short, to co-operate towards the development of the entire country. It is not by presenting such platitudes that we will succeed in proposing a really worthwhile ideal to our youth.
That is a major argument which should compel us to reflect more and to act a little more seriously. Event if we live day by day, we must always think a little further than the tip of our nose. We must always foresee what will happen in six months, in a year, ini two years and even what will happen to future generations, And what about the generations that will be scandalized by the passage of such bills-: it will be a stain- on our political history. That i-s why we insist so much. We have been discussing the problem for three days; in fact, we began the fourth day of discussion- today. We want nobody to say that we have not done our duty, as our constituents asked us to do at the last election.
They demanded that we oppose strongly the- omnibus bill. They also asked all candidates in Quebec to do likewise. That is why

even if we seem to stray from the subject when we ask government members to express their views, we are certain of reflecting the opinion of the majority of the people.
I said the other day, and the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres (Mr. Mongrain) did not seem to believe it, that there is not one person, not one organization that has asked me to support this bill, though it is the subject which has brought forward the greatest volume of mail, and inspired the most discussion. Indeed, we have the support of 100 per cent of the people; mind that: 100 per cent of the people.
Possibly, some may be ready to accept that; 'but none of them ever urged his member to support such a bill.
Mr. Speaker, we have to consider this situation most seriously. The whole country is watching, wondering about the decision we are going to make while aware that with the majority government, we can be forced to-

implications? If we sanction homosexual practices in. any degree, no matter how small, surely we will have great difficulty in maintaining that homosexuality is objectionable in a general or social sense. The defenders: of the amendment creating this new section have made a great thing of saying that it in no way implies official sanction of homosexuality. This1 may be true in a strictly legal sense, but not every young Canadian is a lawyer. There is bound to grow up a general public sense that homosexual practices are all right and tolerable if practised discreetly. In my view this amendment will simply open the door to a gradual acceptance of homosexuality in all its ramifications.
What this amendment says in effect is that homosexual gratification is entirely permissible and quite acceptable in certain circumstances, but in others remains a grave moral and criminal offence. This is a witches' brew. It is: only going to produce confusion in. the public mind and could very possibly lead to legal problems and entanglements far more complicated than those that the amendment seeks' to get rid of.
The trouble is that homosexual practices will no longer be completely forbidden nor completely sanctioned. The amendment is neither fish, fowl nor good red meat. It is a timid half-way measure that will satisfy neither those who hold that homosexuality in any form is an abomination, nor those reformers who regard it as a regrettable human aberration that is more a disease than a crime and something that should be removed from the Criminal Code in its entirety. I believe this amendment to be a weak compromise between rigid rejection by our society of homosexuality in all its manifestations, and the wide open, completely permissive society sought by radical reformers.
It would be interesting to know whether our legal authorities have been able to come up with any figures on the rate of conversion of young people to homosexual practices. I am not aware of any such figures but I believe they are a critical factor in the consideration of this amendment. I believe so because, after all, what we will be saying to our young people from now on, if this legislation carries, is that homosexuality is criminal and abhorrent but only up to the age of 21. There is something particularly absurd in setting an arbitrary age frontier of 21.
I would like to go back for a minute to the conversion rate of young people to homosexuality. It has always been stated that homosexuals are not criminals but are sick. This may 29180-491a

or may not be true. But are not kleptomaniacs sick? Are not a great many murderers sick? Are not rapists sick, and a great many other people involved in crimes? But the fact remains that our laws are made to protect law-abiding normal citizens, whether it be from people who are sick or people who are unfortunate in some other way.
The argument has been made that the homosexual must be protected from blackmail. Surely our young people also deserve protection. The urge of these people to convert young persons to their ways is established. Let us not forget this. There are doubts in my mind whether homosexuals are in reality sick to the extent that is often presented in their favour. Homosexual practices are common in prisons where men are without women and vice-versa. They often occur in private schools where groups of men are shut up together for long periods of time. Does this make them sick? Where I come from people have a different terminology for such actions.
The minister needs to bear in mind that not all homosexuals are sick. Some may be sick, but there are a variety of reasons why people are this way. Definitely not all these people are sick, and I maintain that the law should remain as a deterrent, that the law is to protect average citizens, those who believe in the natural processes.
There are other things such as male prostitution to which this amendment will open the door. As long as consenting adults can carry on legally provided they do so in private, this is a very distinct possibility. There are so many ramifications to this whole problem that I believe we should strike out this amendment and go back to an extensive and scientific study of the whole problem in all its aspects. Such a serious and far-reaching social problem should not be tampered with as one small part of a large, omnibus amendment of the Criminal Code. For all I or anyone else in Canada knows, a thorough study of the question might indicate that homosexuality should be removed entirely from the realm of criminal law and treated as a social welfare problem, as are human weaknesses such as tuberculosis, mental illness, etc. As far as I can see all this amendment does is make things easier for some lawyers and judicial officers, without getting at the root of the problem in any comprehensive way. In doing so it will open the door to many possible developments which at this time we can only conjecture.
While I am on the subject of amendments to the Criminal Code, may I say I wonder

April 21, 1969
Criminal Code
why more significant amendments were not undertaken when so many subjects were under review. For instance, It would be interesting to hear from the minister whether his departmental officials have studied the legalizing of prostitution. I do not have the report at hand at the moment, but I recall seeing the results of a study carried on in an area of the United States where prostitution was legalized. This action resulted in a dramatic and I might say very welcome drop in crimes such as rape, muggings, sex murders and things of that nature. I would think the minister would be well advised to look into this aspect. It seems to me that the problem of increasing crimes of violence, sex offences and crimes in the streets generally should have a higher priority in terms of legal reform than should minor facets such as homosexuality, abortion and the like.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
I do not wish to labour the subject any further, but it does seem to me that with this amendment creating a new section 149A the minister has laboured long and strenuously and brought forth a mouse. At best it does no more than scratch the surface of a tremendous social question. At worst it provides semi-official sanction for a practice which the majority of civilized people still regard with revulsion. It may be quite clear to lawyers that this amendment does not constitute official sanction, but to the majority of Canadians untrained in the law and unable to judge its delicate nuances it will come to mean that the government of Canada no longer regards homosexuality and homosexual practices as offences against our social code. Whatever the legal profession and the judiciary may say, the adoption of this amendment will be taken generally as meaning that this practice has official approval.
Because I believe that any good this amendment will do will be far outweighed by its bad effects I suggest its withdrawal. In making this suggestion I would close by repeating what I said earlier, that the whole subject of homosexuality be taken up by somebody competent to study all its aspects and its position in our modern Canadian society today. To my mind this would be a sounder and more civilized approach to a question that most people admit is a huge and growing social problem.

Mr. Speaker, the spectacle the House of Commons

is presently giving of itself to the country with the discussion of the bill on homosexuality is rather sad judging from reactions which have been coming in from several areas of the country.
We must admit that sometimes humans are even more bestial than animals.
If possible, I would like the people to know through our media of information what we think of homosexuality.
Practically everyone agrees that homosexuality is a disease. Therefore, instead of making it legal, why not bring forward a bill aiming to build hospitals where those sick people could be treated? I suggest we should take this course instead of introducing in the house a bill allowing adults to commit such acts together.
I said a minute ago that human bestiality is more stupid than animal bestiality. As a matter of fact, when has one seen two elks or two bears play together?
There is an animal species, the rabbits, called the hot race. When has anyone seen two adult rabbits practise homosexuality or sexual bestiality? Never, because they know it is not the natural thing to do.
Mr. Speaker, we, who are reasonable people, have initiated in the house a debate to determine whether homosexuality should be legalized, whether we should allow two men or two women twenty-one years of age and over to have fun together, if they fell that way. That is more stupid than animal bestiality.
Mr. Speaker, they want to sanction such bestiality by means of a national act. As my colleague from Champlain (Mr. Matte) said a while ago: the population is against. Who suggested to the Minister of Justice, two years ago, that is so the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), who exerted pressures on him to have such a bill introduced in the house?
We see quite clearly that the measure should not only be up-do-date but also act as a sort of preventive medicine.
A while ago, my colleague from Champlain eloquently said that that bill is intended for our 16, 17 or 18 year-olds; but let them wait until they are 21 years old, and then they can give free rein to their instincts.
And to think, Mr. Speaker, that an educational program could so easily be set up right across Canada to correct that situation. There are so many beautiful women and young girls who are looking for husbands as handsome, if
April 21. 1969

possible, as the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) who would be all too glad to settle for a happy wedded life.
But, Mr. Speaker, instead of introducing a bill to educate the young, to encourage them to marry, and to give them the economic context in which they could found a family, the government invites them, through legislation, to prepare for homosexuality when they reach the age of freedom, 21. To think that we should lose such handsome men and beautiful women through the fault of the Department of Justice!
Mr. Speaker, we are not the only members who feel this way for some government members think exactly as we do. Not only are they afraid to speak up, but they have been forbidden to do so because the bill must be passed at any cost. There will be no free vote on this matter, because the existence of the government would be at stake; so the government demands that its "followers" vote for the bill.
I know government members who represent French-Canadian ridings, for instance, in the province of Quebec; they have received hundreds of protests against this bill. But they are too lazy or too cowardly to get up and say so. We are accused, we, of the Rallie-ment creditiste, of playing politics with this issue. Did we introduce this dreadful bill in the house? No, Mr. Speaker, we did not ask the government to introduce this bill.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
Even before discussing the omnibus bill we asked that it be split. The government said no, take it or leave it. Of course, I expect that members will vote as a groups on those clauses. The government has an absolute majority, and it will have its bill adopted. However, let us not fancy that the Canadian people as a whole will accept it.
I have just come back from a tour in Western Canada I have visited Vancouver, Edmonton, Regina and Winnipeg, and received several telephone calls following radio and television broacasts from persons who termed the bill as inhuman. I know there are sick people, but in that case, there is only one thing to do, and it is to cure them.
I received a few telephone calls from homosexuals who are in favour of the bill. They did not ask me to meet them, but, they told me it was a problem for them and that if they were now caught in the act, they might lose their job.

Mr. Speaker, there might be an answer to their problem. Let us make them work longer hours and they will have less time to indulge in homosexuality. In my opinion, that would settle the problem. This legislation will not prevent them from practising homosexuality; on the contrary, it will merely sanction it.
That is why the Ralliement Creditiste strongly objects to the passing of this bill.
There are homosexuals in all classes of society. There are some even in colleges and universities. There are some even among the members of religious orders. We all know that; the fact remains that the homosexual act is still against nature, inhuman and, as I said earlier, very stupid. It is a form of "human bestiality" which is more stupid that "animal bestiality". I am convinced of it.
Mr. Speaker, the first thing to do in order to standardize human behaviour is to promote education. Instead of the CBC showing us television programs dealing with homosexuality, hippies, or people who live make a living from that, why not use the mass media such as television and the press to educate the adults?
We would thus be educating the young people who are growing up, our own children, instead of cramming their minds with the notion that at 21 they can engage in homosexual acts in all confidence.
In fact, Mr. Speaker, why not educate our youth? We refuse to spend money for education. We would be very happy to see every day, on the public network, the Minister of Justice educating the people in this respect. If he is not familiar with this field, let the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) undertake this job.
Thanks to television, radio and the press we could make the people understand that homosexuality is a disease, that it is curable and that it is possible to see the light.
We appeal not to the beast but to the reason of the beast. The government does not want to do anything. From time to time on television the Minister of Justice states that his legislation will change nothing, that the situation will not deteriorate further, that from now on homosexuals will not be put in jail and that it will be very well that way.
Let me state that the situation will change because this legislation invites the young people of 15, 16 and 17 years of age to engage in homosexual acts when they reach the age of 21. Why? Because the economic conditions

which prevent them from entering into marriage, will oblige them to take their pleasure among men or among women.
Mr. Speaker, are we stupid enough to believe that man has been made for man? The good Lord created woman for man. God created man and woman; that is normal, natural and proper.
It is good.

A Liberal, Mr. Speaker, tells me it is good. He is right.
Mr. Speaker, here is our point of view: for the last three or four days, my colleagues have been objecting to the passing of this bill. People think we are bores. They say: the Ralliement creditiste delays the work of the house. But it is really quite simple, we would not delay the house if this1 legislation were amended, so as not to forcibly legalize homosexuality. I repeat that homosexuality is perennial. It will exist fifty years from now, as it existed fifty years ago. But that does not mean' that we should legalize it, because we would be transgressing the laws' of nature.
Such is my opinion of the bill before us.
Animals do not do such things and we are rational animals. Nobody will convince me that the difference between reason and absence of reason lies in homosexuality.
If that is the difference, we should be ashamed of being rational beings.
Mr. Speaker, this goes against nature. Reason is being devalorized the introduction of such a bill is based upon bestial motive.
The Ralliement creditiste will keep up its opposition to such a bill. No matter whether it lasts one week, two or three weeks or even a month, we shall do everything possible to prevent the passing of this bill. Closure alone would stop our fight against that bill which I call diabolical.

Mr. Speaker, I did not initially anticipate participating in this debate and certainly I will not do so unduly this afternoon. I say this for a reason advanced by members on both sides of the house during the discussion of the principles and generalities involved in this bin.
Those sections of the bill which are contentious, provocative and sensitive, dealing with abortion, lotteries and homosexuality, involve individual consciences and morality. I certainly agree with the Minister of Justice (Mr. 
Turner), and I do not think there is much disagreement in the house, when he states that law is not morality. Morality depends upon so many things. What you may find moral, Mr. Speaker, with your wisdom, I might find to be of another shade. Morality is an individual thing.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
When this bill came before the house and the debate approached, I was bothered about whether I should speak and contribute what little I can to the debate. If it is a matter of individual conscience and a new morality about which we are talking, be it homosexuality, abortion or lotteries, to name the three main ones, I ask: Can we ever have a consensus of conscience? I thought I had seriously decided not to participate verbally in the debate but to cast my vote and explain my action to my constituents at any time they sought an explanation, and in reply to letters I have received on the various sections of the bill but, having listened to the debate in the last three or four days, some of the loose language used on both sides of the house has bothered me very much and I have decided to say a few words on the subject. We talk about conscience. Some may say that this chamber is the conscience of the nation. On the other hand, having listened to many hon. members speak in the debate it is very obvious that in trying to resolve matters as the conscience of the nation and their collective constituents they are substituting their own consciences. This is not a new problem; members of parliament have faced this dilemma many times in the past. A member knows that the stand he takes may cause irritation, conflict and division in the heartland of his support, namely, his constituency.
In trying to resolve this dilemma it occurred to me that while we talk as the conscience of the nation and try to resolve this problem with our individual consciences, we have the unfortunate situation of members on the government side, for reasons of government policy, not being able to express their own views on the various clauses of the bill. I suppose this is really why I am contributing what little I can to the debate on the clause of the bill dealing with homosexuality. In my opinion this is the most bothersome clause in the bill. The right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) may miss many, if not all, the votes on the bill when they are called. I have another and personal reason in this connection. In my

That will be my reason for not being in the chamber when some of the votes are called. Of all the clauses in the bill, the one dealing with homosexuality gives me most concern. Except for an amendment by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) on the question of lotteries, which I think has some merit, my predisposition as of now is to vote with the government on all sections of the bill other than that dealing with homosexuality. My mind could change, because it has changed since I began listening to the debate. It started to change when I tried to resolve this dilemma of conscience.
People have been using their individual consciences in this debate. Some of my hon. friends have been attacking amendments and trying to impose their own views on others. This is a matter of individual morality, yet there has been no expression of individual morality by members on the other side even though I know they have very individual views on this matter which is not political in the sense of most normal, political issues. It is unfortunate that in an area where politics means nothing, where party labels go out the window, we have not heard expressions of individual conscience from members on both sides. If we had, we might have a more relevant appreciation of what is the real conscience of the nation on this question.
We have not yet heard a member speak in support of any form of homosexuality or lesbian conduct. Let us not forget that women are involved in this matter. This type of conduct has to be performed between two consenting adults. The only thing the chamber has heard about for the last four days is homosexuality, but let us not forget that there are lesbians in this country. This type of conduct is not normal and no one has approved of it.
Are we the conscience of the nation, representing our respective constituencies? How can we radiate that conscience when the largest block of voters, not the majority of voters, is represented by those members from the great urban areas of Canada who have not been allowed to speak? I appreciate that my hon. friends in the New Democratic party support holus-bolus the amendments in this
Criminal Code
bill. They have given us an expression of opinion. The Creditistes and many members of the Official Opposition have spoken on this question and the dialogue has been joined. We have heard expressions of opinion sincerely held.
If there was anything that brought me into the debate it was the debate of Friday last when I listened to two speeches on this provocative and emotional issue. Those two speeches will be remembered for some time by this junior member. One was the speech of the right hon. member for Prince Albert, expressed in his particular style, a style that we shall perhaps not see too much of in the house in the future because of the problems of getting elected for some 20 years in this day and age. That type of speech actually may not glorify this place, but it adds lustre to it. The other speech was that of the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) who has a completely different debating style. But for once in this debate the dialogue was joined and their two views on the question of homosexuality were expressed in vivid, colourful, and in most cases logical language. Therefore, one in a dilemma could perhaps make up his mind.
I give full credit to the hon. member for York South and his ability as one of the real debaters in this chamber. However, unfortunately, in my opinion, he put forward a very specious argument. He castigated those who are against the amendment. He suggested that anyone who questions the amendment must be living in an antediluvian state. He castigated members of the opposition for their self-righteous or sanctimonious approach to the problem. In my opinion it adds nothing to this debate to use such adjectives about sincerely held views. If this amendment is passed, I could say it will introduce another, new Liberal law of licentiousness. But that is specious reasoning and I do not intend to maintain it further.
I do not think the cause of this amendment is helped when, for whatever reason, the minister of Justice refuses to admit that in effect its purport is to legalize homosexuality. The fact is that the amendment takes away a prohibition that at the present time makes this type of conduct illegal. My colleague on this side of the house who spoke before me said he was not a lawyer. I happen to be versed in the law to a degree, although not with the ability and experience of the Minister of Justice. However, I cannot understand why the minister should be specious in respect of what is in my opinion the substance

Criminal Code
of the bill. The amendment will give legal sanction to this type of conduct, and if it gives legal sanction then, ipso facto, by implication it legalizes this type of sexual act. If I referred earlier to abortion, Mr. Speaker, that was not my intention; I am concerned now only with the aspects of the bill relating to homosexuality.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
The hon. member for York South, in talking about the proposal in connection with homosexuality, stated both inside and outside the house that every progressive western country had enacted such a law. But the only two countries I have heard mentioned in this debate are Great Britain and Sweden. I am not saying we should never be among the avant-garde or that we should never lead the way, provided there is a tremendous body of public opinion behind us to show that an advance is necessary. The hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie (Mr. Murphy) told us that he got sanction for this position when he ran in the election last June. I must say I do not recall this issue as being among the election planks upon which the voters were asked to express an opinion.
The hon. member for York South told us, as I mentioned, that every advanced western country had adopted a provision along the lines proposed to this parliament. Yet the only two countries mentioned in this connection, to my knowledge, were Sweden and Brit-ian. Frankly, I am not over-enamoured by either the social or political conduct of those countries. Surely we in Canada can map out our own lines of social conduct. We do not need to lean on those, in my opinion, weak reeds. We were not told that New Zealand, Australia or any of the states of the United States had enacted legislation along the lines now proposed to us.
During this debate many speakers have sought to justify this amendment on the ground that today we are living in a pluralistic society. This is another catch phrase which is being bandied about increasingly. It is said we cannot define standards of morality because we live in a pluralistic society. What does the phrase "pluralistic society" mean? In itself it is meaningless, rather like that other expression, "don't let the state into the bedroom"-good public relations, maybe, but nothing else. The state does enter the bedroom every time we turn on the television set in the bedroom. Programs are under state regulation, even though it may not be the kind of regulation we would like. If a man

kills his wife in the bedroom the state will not remain outside.
What does "pluralistic society" mean? What kind of division does it imply? I do not care how pluralistic our society may he, or how many streams enter into it. It does not matter to me how many English-speaking, Frenchspeaking, Greek-speaking or Italian-speaking citizens make up our society. I believe it is one Canada though it has problems, but that the plurality of the different streams contained in it makes no difference to the setting up of a philosophy of law or a concept of morality. Ever since the Judaeo-Christian concept spread through a large part of the world, western nations particularly have developed a concept of morality and a philosophy of law based on this understanding. Yet there are those who would destroy this on the ground that we live in a pluralistic society. Reasoning of this type is specious and only confuses the issue.
The hon. member for York South was quite eloquent and, at one point, almost vicious in his criticism of my right hon. friend from Prince Albert, maintaining that my right hon. friend had destroyed his credibility as a defender of civil liberties in Canada because he held an interpretation of morality different from that held by the hon. member for York South. The hon. member for York South is himself renowned as a defender of civil liberties, yet I founid his contribution to this debate to be surprisingly weak.
I would remind hon. members that we shall later be considering a clause concerning the proposed breathalyzer test, something which will come closer to Canadians and involve the civil liberties of more Canadians than all this talk about homesexuality or lesbian conduct. This is an area in which civil liberties are directly involved. Yet it is private conduct. The minister shakes his: head. I agree it is not private conduct when a man takes his car and gets into an accident. But we propose going much farther. As I understand the amendment, it is to be an offence if a driver refuses to take a test.
I do not say I am against such a provision. Indeed, I would be prepared to accept it. I agree that statistics have shown a definite connection between liquor and the slaughter on the highways. The law is bound to move into this area, even though it cannot put an end to drinking. But if we are logical, and if we are talking about civil liberties, here is an area of definite concern. Under the new law it will be an offence to refuse to take a test. Yet private conduct is involved, and a
April 21, 1969

Criminal Code
driver who has taken the two or three one-ounce drinks, all that are necessary, will produce the reading of .08 which is sufficient to justify further proceedings.
I could be driving my car straight down the highway and straight into my own driveway-and it would be driven straight; I could be stepping out of the car, and a policeman could say: I suspect you came from that party at the Skyline last year during the Liberal convention and there just might have been some alcohol available there so I want to take a reading. I could tell him: I have only two steps to take before reaching my house, officer. I am glad you followed me. I did not exceed the speed limit. I did not wander over the white line. I just want to enter my house, kiss my wife and greet my children. So I shall say goodbye to you. His reply is likely to be: You cannot do that under the new law. You are committing an offence if you do not come to the police station and have a reading taken.
I am prepared to accept this restriction on my civil liberties because statistics show there is a real connection between drinking and driving. While there are no statistics to serve as a guide when we are considering the problem of homosexuality, I remind the house that no one who has spoken in the debate has approved of these practices. They have all expressed repugnance to them. If we can agree to restrict civil liberties in connection with alcohol, why cannot we take the collective opinion expressed by members of this chamber and say that, through we cannot legislate morality, surely we can help define morality and in this way give expression to the repugnance voiced by all hon. members who have spoken so far.
Members of the N.D.P. in particular have talked about justifying these proposals on sociological grounds. Reference was made to blackmail by the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Downey). There is no reason for there to be either more blackmail or less blackmail as a result of the passing of this amendment. I recall one case in my practice of a person who was being blackmailed. But it was not because of anything in the Criminal Code. The man was being blackmailed because of his conduct-conduct which the Minister of Justice himself says is abhorrent, repugnant and immoral. Why cannot we continue to use this provision as a means of defining morality?
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
I am not saying that this problem should be solved by imposing legal sanction or that there should not be a clause in the bill providing that somebody found guilty of this conduct should be punished. In fact, I should like the minister to tell me whether anybody has ever been charged under this section of the code. If you have two consenting males, who is going to squeal? In any event, I am not saying that legal sanction should be the way to attack this problem. I agree with my hon. friend from Battle River that there are other avenues of approach. Perhaps we should amend the bill to provide that anybody so found guilty should be given psychiatric treatment. Let the problem be investigated so we can ascertain what is involved.
Hon. members have mentioned many aspects of this problem. Unless something is substituted for the removal of the legal sanction, you cannot help but lessen the moral stigma. I have not heard one member say that this conduct is moral. I would vote against this homosexuality clause because it does not go to the root of the problem while at the same time it removes the legal sanction against offences with respect to which there have been no prosecutions. This amendment will make for misinterpretation and, as I said, will certainly lessen the moral stigma.

Mr. Speaker, this afternoon, we have to study amendments moved by the hon. members for Abitibi and Calgary North (Messrs. Laprise and Woolliams). Those amendments would require no debate if the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) had wanted to take the advice given him at the time of the introduction of this omnibus bill, when it was suggested to him to remove the clauses concerning homosexuality and abortion.
If both those clauses had been removed from this shameful bill, we would not have wasted three days protesting.
Do perverted promoters, free thinkers who tolerate homosexuals, think they justify themselves and the government of Canada, by saying that only the government is responsible for intimidating homosexuals by means of corrective justice if the act is committed in private between consenting adults? It is precisely an impure act committed with the mutual consent of participants.

April 21, 1969
Criminal Code
We put the following question: Can the government depart from its moral responsibility to the extent of showing no concern at all for the deterioration and the disintegration of our whole social structure? And can the Canadian Government, by renouncing its responsibilities with regard to these problems, escape the blame of encouraging immorality?
Our society is a fragile, artificial creation, designed as a whole, not by natural permanent forces, but by a man-made code of morality, based on Christian ethics.
Society is strongly opposed to sodomy, as it punishes murder or theft, because it strikes at its roots, namely the family. It is nonsensical to pretend, as our legislators do, that society can do without something which affects its own existence. One might as well argue that murder, as it affects the duration of life, could be left to the individual conscience, if one admits that homosexuality, which also affects life, could also be so classified.
A resurgence of homosexuality and an increasing tolerance of its practices are unseparable from a declining civilization, are the stigmas of a decaying civilization. Being the symptom of immorality and of a serious social ill, it speeds up the disruption of the whole social structure.
In the decaying cultures of Great Britain and Europe, such a state of mind has influenced the arts and recreation, showing itself in utterly aggressive exhibitionism, under the guise of a dazzling revolution.
Literature is poisoning the mind of young Canadians and Americans, where it is making common cause with drug addicts and beatniks.
In spite of the avowed pragmatism of its supporters, the bill designed to legalize homosexuality in Canada is a menace not only to young people, to parents and families, but also to society.
To condone such repugnant and socially bad morals is to deprive this young and virile nation of its most precious heritage.
I had the chance of hearing some of his observations.
I have here a letter from the Thetford Mines chief of police. In it, he writes, and I quote:
Last April 3rd, twenty (20) chiefs of police of the Eastern townships region made a study of it-
He means the bill omnibus.
I therefore send you a list of the amendments we propose, with a view to facilitating the application of that law and to serving better the public we have the duty to protect-

We have the right to propose amendments, because the bill should never have been introduced.
They would have several amendments to propose regarding the bill omnibus, and here is what he has to say about that:
That clause 7, amending sections 147 and 149, be amended by deleting paragraph (b); that is, the words "any two persons, each of whom is twenty-one years or more of age".
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
We are asked, in the light of the findings of serious studies made by police chiefs, to strike out those words at least, because this bill which, in our opinion, should not be passed, is now at a stage where we can only move amendments. Therefore, I ask the movers of this legislation to seriously consider the findings of those studies.
Moreover, I know that the conscience of several hon. members is being tortured these days. That of the Minister of Justice is, because he must go on defending his bill. He would have preferred to amend it but because of his party's tyranny, he must toe the line.
We have talked with several government members and I wonder why they hesitate so much to express their opinion freely in this house because some of them say that they would like to be allowed to vote according to their conscience.
In expressing such an opinion, they sometimes give the impression that they vote without considering their conscience and they are forced to submit to the guidelines of the party. In the presence of such obstinacy on the part of the government that takes decisions and forces government members to comply with them without a word, we are justified in asking ourselves whether there is not something hidden in that bill that nobody wants.
In fact, I do not see why, if it is so sure of the quality of its legislation, the government would not trust its members. If they consider the bill adequate and consistent with their conscience, they would not object to it and the Minister of Justice would be well advised to clarify things in that matter, if only to ease the conscience of those poor members who are forced to obey without a word.
In the field of homosexuality it must be kept in mind that even today, when two homosexuals want to commit such acts privately, nobody will denounce them and no sentence will be passed on them. It is only when one of them has a grievance that he will be able to lodge a complaint.
April 21, 1969

And if one of them is not consenting, the omnibus bill will not apply. Therefore, the omnibus bill does not bring anything constructive in the field of homosexuality. At best, it will create a climate of doubt and uncertainty, which will protect the active pervert and guilty homosexual. He will be the only one to lose by it and if there is no consent, I cannot see why we are being led to believe that this bill is going to change anything.
I think we are now at the cross-roads of history. And we, Canadians, should look back on the past, at the way our ancestors lived and ask ourselves whether the latter would not think we have indeed departed from the most sacred principles of our faith, if they could hear us now discussing this bill.
I am sure they are ashamed of us and that if we continue to give in, they will raise from their tombs, to put us back in the path of honour. Let us not put out the torch of faith which they passed on to us, at the cost of so many sacrifices and of so much blood. I believe that a nation which fails to remember is a dying nation, because one never builds the future of a country by disowning its history.
I cannot understand how one could be justified in voting for this bill. We must at least adopt those amendments and I am urging every one of our leaders to express their views since we are responsible for the wellbeing of our people and are able to do what is necessary in order to preserve moral values while there is still time.
I say: Let us not allow the morality of our people to deteriorate, let us not allow such evil depravity through legislation.
Therefore, I appeal to the Minister of Justice to amend this bill on homosexuality, if he wants Canada to remain the country which has produced so many valuable things.

Mr. Speaker, I also want to express my opinion and support the amendments moved by the hon. members for Abitibi and Calgary North (Messrs. Laprise and Woolliams).
I believe it will be a historical day for Canadians in general, if this bill is passed, because it seems to me that morals in this country will be rather debased.
Mr. Speaker, as a member of the committee on agriculture, I made a trip to the western provinces. Having seen all the work done to raise cattle of the highest quality, through better cross-breeding, we are coming back to
Criminal Code
parliament most pleased with our trip, only to deal with a matter that is so much against nature as cross-breeding between men and between women, and that leads me to say the next generation will not be worth much. No western farmer will vote for such crossbreeding. Having heard what we were told in the west about the qualifications pertaining to males and females, I believe that our reasonable Canadian race is becoming a race of poor quality.
Mr. Speaker I really feel sorry as I rise to take part in this debate this afternoon, because, along with my colleagues, I strongly opposed that bill on its introduction by the present Prime Minister, and we have kept asking that the whole matter be not put together in the same package so that Canadian Christian Catholics will not be forced to pocket such an affront, because they still believe in morals, even human morals. We have always asked the present Prime Minister to split up the bill, but we were refused.
When the justice portfolio changed hands, we felt happy, for we trusted the present minister more than the former one, since we are aware of his stubbornness. We hoped that the present minister of Justice, who is a father and has moral principles, would simply strike out these two clauses from the omnibus bill; but we realize in great despair that the head of the Department of Justice is actually not the present minister but the Prime Minister, who still exerts dictatorial authority over it. The minister has been unable to change the least thing in that famous bill initiated by the Prime Minister.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
Mr. Speaker, I have no desire to crush the Minister of Justice. In fact, I am sorry for him, and if it were possible to weep for him I think that many hon. members would do it today. It seems to me that because of this party dictatorship which muzzles all cabinet members this clause will pass automatically since this is a majority government.
That is why in campaigning throughout the country the Liberal party said: give us an absolute majority and you will see how we shall govern. They won an absolute majority but I think the people will repent bitterly for the rest of their life.
When such filth is brought before us-and I call that filth without wince-I think that acts so much against nature should not even be discussed by any self-respecting government.

April 21, 1963
Criminal Code
But what can be done? This matter has to be dealt with since it has been brought before the house. They do not want to let it go. Here is a small bundle of rot which they do not want to part with. They want others to taste it.
Mr. Speaker, I think that the first one who is going to try to have me taste it, will be putting his life in danger. Yet other members must have received letters of protest since I have received some myself-over 1,500 of my electors asked me to object and to try to get these two clauses at least deleted.
But the cabinet members will not speak. It looks as if they have not received any letter. However, I have read rather eloquent reports in the newspapers. I shall not speak of letters I have received from my ridings since they will say that I have indoctrinated my electors.
I have collected some letters and statements published in newspapers outside my constituency which anyone can read. One of those articles was entitled: "Letter to the member of parliament" and had been sent by the Association of graduate nurses of Saint-Henri, Levis constituency. The hon. member for Levis has certainly received some protests. This is what the article says:
As for homosexuals, it is possible that some of them are suffering from mental illness which the state must detect and cure, but it is not the majority. You know quite well, the more the law will be permissive in that respect, the more corrupters there will be who will endeavour to take our youth along the road to perdition and moral depravity.
If druggists were authorized to sell to anyone, without prescription, heroin, marijuana, etc ... would there be fewer or more drug addicts? The answer is clear, is it not? If all obstacles are removed, vices and crimes will spread more than ever.
One must not forget that sodomy was the direct cause of the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrha and that the decay of morals in ancient Rome led to the fall of the Roman Empire. Every day, one can increasingly note the fast decay of morals in North America, the disintegration of the family, the increasing ease with which one can get a divorce, the surrender of the citizens, parents and even elected representatives before their most essential duties-
I think that this nurse knew that her member of parliament was a Liberal.
The letter goes on:
-we ask ourselves in terror if the hand of God will not weigh heavy on us, as it did on Europe through two horrible wars within fifty years.
In the name of heaven, stand up and unite with all French-Canadian and English-Canadian members of parliament, whether they be Catholic or Christian against those iniquitous laws, because

the law of God must prevail over partisan or government solidarity, public and individual interests.
You may rest assured that all the people, particularly in the province of Quebec, will think more highly of you.
It is signed:
R.S.D., registered nurse
Saint-Henri,
Ldvis County
I believe in the riding of Levis there has certainly been some opposition. The letter I read did not come from my constituency or that of Lapointe, but from the riding of Levis.
No.

The hon. member for
Lapointe says he did not receive any letter. His constituents are intelligent; I find it strange that they have not yet found his address.
Now, Mr. Speaker, we would like to hear government members state their reasons for endorsing the bill. Then, we could show the transcript of their speeches to their electors and tell them: that is what they think. But there is no way of knowing, because they remain silent.
Mr. Speaker, I have before me a document prepared by La Ligue des citoyens et proprietaries de Boucherville which takes exception to the bill on homosexuality. The member for Boucherville must have received it even though his electors may not know his address. (Laughter) In case he has not found the time to read it, I am going to do so, and I quote:
Please find herewith copy of a letter sent to Canada's Prime Minister, Mr. L. B. Pearson, and to members of the House of Commons-
Mr. Pearson is mentioned because the present Prime Minister was then Minister of Justice. The letter goes on:
La Ligue des citoyens et proprietaires de Boucherville Inc. has decided, during a regular meeting, to advise the House of Commons that they object to the bill on homosexuality.
It has been resolved that matters of a much more urgent nature were pressing the members of parliament than legislation on sexual offences committed by perverted persons. We feel that it is much more urgent to look after normal citizens which form a majority than to pass legislations for a small, albeit influent group, in order to legalize acts against nature.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to point out that I do not quote this article because the member concerned is here but rather because I came across it by chance. I do not want him to think that I hold any grudge against him because I
April 21, 1969

quote articles that have been published in his constituency. As a matter of fact, I hold him in high esteem and there are many respectable people in his constituency.
We respectfully submit that parliament should deal rather with the housing problem and the homeowners' situation-
I simply wish to advise their M.P. that they categorically object to homosexuality as well as to other provisions of the omnibus bill.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
I have before me a very important article -but time will not permit me to read it all- dealing with homosexuality, when it was discussed in England. So, as many like to follow in England's footsteps, I shall quote part of the article.
The lesson taught to the provincial Liberal party will have been useless! This catchall proposal, where the good and the horrible are found side by side (no doubt this is a trick to have the whole package approved) will turn into a second hara-kiri for the Liberals ... Too bad!
To induce and help reflection, other than the one-way consideration given the matter by the three guests on the program "AUJOURD'HUI" on the CBC's French network, on December 27, I would like to summarize two articles; the first, dealing with homosexuality, was written by Raymond Lacoste and published in Carrefour (Paris) when the British Parliament was debating a legislative proposal that has now become law, and the second, dealing with abortion, being a study made by the High Committee on Population and Family of France.
To legalize homosexuality?
On February 11 last, the British Parliament adopted a legislative proposal legalizing homosexuality. Raymond Lacoste, a Parisian journalist, comments-
The debate has brought to light the seriousness of the problem. There are from 50 to 60 million unnatural acts committed each year. The number of sexual crimes which, in 1939, stood at 5,000 per year, reached, in 1964, 20,000; during the same period and later-
Statistics are given-
23,470 while criminal offences reached a total of 303.000 to-
I do not know if an investigation was being carried out in the bedrooms, but apparently, there was some accounting made of all such things!
I continue:
An honest Labour member, Mr. Tommy, went on to say: I protest against the tone of alleged intellectual superiority adopted by the supporters of the bill. What they are asking, in a word, is that we give approval to male prostitution, when, a few years ago, parliament dealt severely with
Criminal Code
female prostitutes and gave chase to call-girls. Today, through some strange mental aberration, British legislators are showing more indulgence for acts against nature than for acts that, although sinful, are after all normal!
Raymond Lacoste goes on in some grimly humourous way which should make us cry instead of laugh:
"Grave" consideration was the order of the day during the debates. Needless to say that, when the vote was taken, the beautiful young men with mascaraed eyes who filled the galleries broke into applause so great was their joy!
The defenders of the dear boys put forward all sorts of arguments .. . Very soberly, Mr. Wood stated that homosexuality does not carry with it the risk of illegitimate births! Why send an uranist to prison? Is that not the same as condemning a Don Juan to a few years in a harem? (This argument put forward by Mr. Absi, a member, gave rise to laughter among his colleagues.)
There were strong objections to the bill. Some speakers showed the nonsense of a system which will authorize men of 21 years of age to commit an act while punishing individuals 20 years and 10 months old. But the promoters of the legislation insisted that there was no reason to deal more harshly with homosexuals than with lesbians who have their own club. They are spared by the British law. Many speakers emphasized the nature of complete demoralization caused by the gidian vice and its damage to society.

Criminal Code
Parole Act, the Penitentiary Act, the Prisons and Reformatories Act and to make certain consequential amendments to the Combines Investigation Act, the Customs Tariff and the National Defence Act, as reported (with amendments) from the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs, and the motion of Mr. McQuaid (for Mr. Woolliams):

[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)

Mr. Speaker, I take pleasure in participating in this debate because of its great importance. However many members and some ministers consider it of little importance. This vital question is related to another moral issue which affects the existence of men and the respect they command in society.
Mr. Speaker, if our Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) are stupid enough to introduce legislation as bad and as indecent as this one, they should be expelled from parliament. This is no ordinary legislation which we are now considering, but degrading legislation which will lead our nation to suicide.
Knowledgeable people like the Minister of Justice and the Prime Minister have the nerve to introduce a piece of legislation as indecent and as degrading as this one. Mr. Speaker, we cannot find words harsh enough to describe there criminal actions which we are about to allow.
Mr. Speaker, this is what we are doing now. Here is patent evidence of irresponsibility on the part of the Liberal members. They will pay dearly for their mistakes. Someone will have to pay for all that. We have no right to impose upon the nation such legislation. It is immoral, unchristian, antisocial, inhuman and against anything you want.
All Liberal members are in favour of that. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) as well as a great many opposition members favour the passing of this bill. They consider themselves as saviours of the people. According to them, they promote the establishment of a just society. At the moment we are really degrading society. That is what we are doing. That is What the Liberals, the Progressive

Conservatives and the NDP members are doing now. Somebody will pay for all that. Such social injustice cannot last any longer. Somebody will pay because justice will follow its course. This degrading legislation will lead many individuals to destruction. They will lose their freedom, their personal identity, respect for others if they abase themselves so far as to commit such indecent acts. On account of this disreputable legislation, many citizens will lose 'their moral sense. The permanent stains on people's conscience are caused by the commission of those inhumane acts on account of the passing of those corrupting measures. The passing of such immoral, diabolical, corrupting and rotten measures will turn everything into muck under the nose of those who advocate them and share the opinions of those who are already in such situations and think it smells nice.
We are abusing the confidence of the society we should reform, which gave us the power to administer it, to lead it in the right direction and the necessary authority to provide it with real freedom, so that it may become a just society, a stainless, uncorrupted, pure society. We are not attending to our duty. We are degrading society because we do not want to assume our responsibilities. Some prefer to be led by partisanship.
I have here, Mr. Speaker, a letter I would like to read to the house. It was sent by a citizen of my constituency. Some members may say they did not get anything from their fellow-citizens in that regard, because the latter know that those members will not object to the passing of this bill.
As for me, Mr. Speaker, people know I am opposed to it. I have in my office more than 1,000 letters that were sent to me. I am going to read one of them. All the people writing to me beg me to stand against the legalization of such acts of barbarism.
In fact, I should like to table all those letters I received, if I were allowed to do so. The citizens also tell me I can give their names. As a matter of fact, one of them says in his letter he is not afraid of Showing his convictions. He is a great man, a great Christian. I quote:
If I had to vote-
-on this bill, I would vote against it, since the Prime Minister does not want to split it up into several parts. However, there are certainly many good things in this bill; but since the wheat has been mixed voluntarily with the tares, when
April 21, 19G9

it would be so easy to separate them, in conscience, I would have to vote against it.
Incidentally, by refusing to split up this bill into several parts, the Prime Minister violates-
-the Minister of Justice also.
-the conscience of his members; they have to choose between their conscience and their loyalty to the party.
I fear very much that within the Liberal party especially, the cowardice
-of the Liberals...
-in front of a Prime Minister who notoriously abuses his authority by failing to respect the conscience of his members, partisanship, and party loyalty will prevail over the duty of conscience. If several Liberal members were brave enough to say frankly to the Prime Minister; "Split up your bill into several parts and you let the members free to vote according to their conscience, or we shall vote against this bill, even if the government is defeated.
We will rather follow the demands of our conscience than those of party solidarity. I am certain that the Prime Minister would then give in. But I doubt very much that there is now in Ottawa, in the Liberal party, a sufficient number of courageous men to succeed in this.
This is what my constituents write me. The government members do not speak of it because they fear that they would never have the courage to express in the house the thinking of their constituents.
The author of the letter also talks of abortion. I will not speak of it, but I will just continue quoting the letter:
As for homosexuality, the state, in the words of Mr. Trudeau himself, wants by this bill to declare itself-incompetent to go into the bedrooms and judge the acts that are taking place there.
There is nothing to object to that except that the State should not allow bedroom privacy to be brought into the limelight.
That is what the passage of this infamous bill will cause to happen: public misbehaviour. And the minister will assume a heavy responsibility, if he refuses to split up and improve this odious bill. I go on quoting:
In short, if this bill legalizing abortion and homosexuality, is passed, public morality will be further degraded.
Is this man right? I shall not disclose his name, but he is a priest.
Mr. Speaker, all the letters I have received are along the same lines. Are people better in my constituency than- in those of government members? If the sectors of the government members or of the Conservative members who are going to pass this bill do not protest, it is perhaps because they are all corrupt also. There is corruption everywhere. Mr. Speaker,
Criminal Code
except in my constituency, where it is nonexistent, and I have just proved it.
So, through this corrupting measure, this stinking measure, as I called it before, we are degrading even more the society that we should make healthier. We are encouraging it to commit those criminal acts. It is an alarming, a shocking and a dreadful situation when people shun their responsibilities, prefer corruption and to run to seed rather than assume their responsibilities.
We should, on the contrary, fight this corruption, this barbarous and unconceivable degradation of the human person, because there is nothing greater or nobler than the human person.
The State should pass salvation laws, moral laws, and educate moralists. In order to heal this dreadful disease of society instead of keeping on corrupting it.
The legislation before us is an odious measure that will bring to their doom countless men who will become devoid of any conscience and any respect for the law. This loathsome law will lead to the degradation of our people and will have a serious impact on the future generations.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
